t: Number of Ways to Build Sturdy Brick Wall: Row-Pattern DP
o: We assemble a wall of the given height out of unit-height rows of exactly width units, drawn from an unlimited supply of the given brick widths; the wall is sturdy when adjacent rows never share an interior joint position (the two ends do not count), and we count sturdy walls modulo 10^9 + 7. For height = 2, width = 3 and bricks [1, 2] there are exactly two sturdy walls, while width = 1 with only a 5-wide brick allows no row at all, yielding 0. The decisive scale observation is that width <= 10, so a row's joint layout is a subset of the 9 interior positions — at most 2^9 = 512 possibilities — regardless of height. Because sturdiness compares only neighboring rows' joint sets, enumerating all row layouts once and running a DP down the height whose state is the previous row's joint bitmask solves the problem efficiently.
k: A row layout is fully described by its set of interior joint positions, encodable as a small bitmask.
Two adjacent rows are compatible iff their joint bitmasks are disjoint; the outer ends never conflict.
With width <= 10 there are at most 2^(width-1) = 512 layouts, so pairwise mask DP is cheap even for height 100.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Row Layouts, Bottom-Up Pairwise DP
a.i: First DFS all ways to tile one row from the available widths, recording each layout's interior-joint bitmask (positions 0 and width are boundaries and never joints). Initialize dp[mask] = 1 for every layout, representing a one-row wall ending in that layout. Each additional level transforms dp by summing, for every new top-row mask m, the counts dp[pm] over masks pm disjoint from m. After height - 1 rounds, summing dp yields the answer modulo 10^9 + 7.
s: Discard brick widths exceeding width and de-duplicate the rest.
DFS compositions of width, appending each completed row as an interior-joint bitmask.
Initialize dp[mask] = 1 for every generated mask.
Repeat height - 1 times: ndp[m] = sum of dp[pm] over all pm with pm AND m == 0.
Return the sum of final dp values modulo 10^9 + 7.
a.t: O(height * P^2) where P <= 2^(width-1) <= 512 is the number of distinct row layouts.
a.sp: O(P) for the layout list and current DP layer.

a.i: The same transition graph can be walked recursively. Define go(left, lastMask) as the number of ways to stack the remaining left rows on top of a row with joint mask lastMask; go sums go(left - 1, m) over layouts m disjoint from lastMask and bottoms out at 1 when no rows remain. Memoization on (left, mask index) keeps the state space at height * P, mirroring the bottom-up complexity while expressing the construction top-down.
s: Generate all single-row joint bitmasks exactly as in the iterative version.
Define go(left, idx): ways to place left more rows above the row whose mask is masks[idx].
Otherwise sum go(left - 1, j) over layouts j whose mask is disjoint from masks[idx], memoizing results.
Answer with the sum of go(height - 1, idx) over all starting layouts.
a.t: O(height * P^2) — the same compatibility graph visited recursively with memoization.
a.sp: O(height * P) for the memo table plus O(width) generation recursion.

w: In an interview, generate the row patterns first and only then reach for DP — the tiny width bound is what makes everything feasible. Pitfalls: treating the two outer ends of the wall as joints that must differ between rows (they must not), forgetting to dedupe or filter oversized bricks before generating, and dropping the modulo on intermediate additions. Note the empty-layout case: if no brick fits within width, the answer is 0 regardless of height. Follow-ups include walls where three consecutive rows must avoid common joints (same framework with a two-row window) or bricks with varying heights.
